review.reviewBody: The Sling bag is excellent. This is the exact kind of bike bag I've been looking for over the past several years and I love being able to utilize my front triangle space. I live in a big city and never leave any gear on my bike when it's unattended. I'm all about bags I can easily take on and off my bike. Chrome's DoubleTrack was way too narrow/small for my taste and the Rapha Mini Messenger was clunky and I didn't like the design. I have a few traditional bikepacking/day-ride frame bags, but they're either a pain to take off and on or they're designed for longer term fixed attachment, and none of them are designed for off-bike carrying. The Garner and Tow Sling is my ideal. It fits all the same gear I typically carry in my 7L Osprey hip pack, but with the bonus that my bike's carrying it instead of me. It's easy to access pockets while riding and looks like a "normal" bag off the bike. Love how well it works whether it's mounted on the bike or on my shoulder.

review.name: Excellent every day carry bag for me
review.reviewBody: I originally bought this just to use with my bicycle, but I've been using it every day now, with or without the bike. It's just a nice, super handy bag for day-to-day use. I think the olive color is great for a guy.

review.name: Very well made
review.reviewBody: Very well made, versatile pack! I use it primarily on my hybrid bike, but also take it off and carry it at times. I appreciate the design and local manufacture!
Love it. Really well made and a design that works for me riding or not. Great everyday bag. I highly recommend. Perfect for airplane.

review.name: JUST THE RIGHT SIZE
review.reviewBody: Not too big, not too small. Fits perfectly on my waist or over my shoulder and holds my daily essentials like phone, glasses, keys, wallet. The size and easy open top gives you easy access to your stuff. I bought two!

before.headline: How to Choose the Right Bag for City Commuting
before.articleBody:
If you live in the city, your commute is more than just getting from point A to point B—it’s part of your daily rhythm. Whether you’re biking, walking, riding the train, or mixing all three, the right bag can turn your commute from a juggling act into a seamless, comfortable, and even stylish experience.
At Garner and Tow, we design adaptable bags that move with you—literally—transitioning from bike to body with ease. Choosing the right bag starts with thinking about how you commute. A cyclist may need a design that attaches securely to a bike rack or handlebars, yet still feels natural to carry off the bike. Those who walk or rely on public transit often benefit from a shoulder or crossbody style that keeps hands free for coffee, phone scrolling, or holding onto a crowded bus railing. And for those whose route changes from day to day, adaptability is key—a bag that quickly shifts between bike mode and body mode will keep up no matter how the morning unfolds.
Of course, a bag’s size matters just as much as its flexibility. City life calls for something that can hold a laptop, lunch, water bottle, and maybe an extra layer without becoming a bulky burden. The ideal bag strikes a balance between capacity and agility, making it easy to weave through crowded sidewalks or squeeze onto a packed train. That’s why our Tow Tote and Garner Bag are designed to carry the day’s essentials while keeping a slim, streamlined profile.
Another factor that can’t be ignored is the weather. Urban skies have a way of shifting from blue to stormy without much warning, so a water-resistant bag with sturdy zippers is your best defense against an unexpected downpour. Protection for your laptop and valuables shouldn’t be an afterthought—it’s a necessity.
Comfort also plays a starring role. If you’re carrying your bag for more than a few blocks, padded straps and balanced weight distribution can make all the difference. For cyclists, that means a secure fit that won’t sway or bounce with every turn. The right bag should feel like part of your body, not a weight you’re constantly adjusting.
And then, of course, there’s style. In the city, you might step off your bike or train straight into a meeting, a coffee date, or dinner with friends. Your bag isn’t just a tool—it’s part of your outfit. A versatile, timeless design ensures you look polished no matter where the day takes you. This is where Garner and Tow bags truly shine: they work in the office, on the street, and everywhere in between. Function and style shouldn’t be a trade-off—you can have both.
The best city commuting bag blends adaptability, comfort, and style, supporting your lifestyle instead of slowing you down. If your daily routine involves biking, walking, or catching the train, choosing a bag that moves with you is one of the smartest investments you can make.
Explore our full collection at garnerandtow.com and find the commuting companion that makes your city days flow

The Duffel


When your day calls for more—more to carry, more places to be, more time in motion—the Duffel rises to the occasion. Designed for life on the go, it’s just as at home on your daily commute as it is on a weekend escape. Take it from the office to the gym without missing a beat, or load it up with groceries on the way home. And when adventure calls, the Duffel is ready. With room for camping gear and bikepacking essentials, it’s built to handle the demands of the trail as easily as the demands of your calendar.


Examples:



All your work items plus gym clothes and shoes


Your weeks groceries 


Work computer and charger plus your haul from the thrift store or book store errand after work


Your sleeping system for camping; the duffel is great for your sleeping bag, pillow, and sleeping pad




The Tote


Some days call for simplicity, and that’s where the Tote shines. With a spacious main compartment and five handy exterior pockets, it keeps your essentials organized and within reach. From commuting across town to swinging by the market or heading out for a casual ride, the Tote is built to keep pace with your everyday rhythm—practical, versatile, and always ready to go.


Examples:



All your work items plus a sweater for the chilly office


Snacks, books, camp chairs, and a bottle of wine




The Sling


For days when you want to travel light, the Sling keeps things simple without sacrificing versatility. It clips neatly to your bike as a frame bag, then transitions effortlessly into a sling you can wear on the go. Compact yet surprisingly roomy, it carries the essentials—your water bottle, notebook, and a few extras—so you’re always ready for the ride, the stop, and everything in between.


Examples:



 Phone, keys wallet, plus a book, and snacks for the road


Camping food for a long weekend




The Pouch


Small but mighty, the Pouch is built to keep your essentials close at hand. Compact yet surprisingly spacious, it organizes the things you reach for most—your wallet, tools, snacks, or tech accessories—without adding bulk. Clip it onto the Duffel or Tote with S-Hooks when you need extra room, or wear it crossbody with the optional strap for a lightweight bag that moves with you. However you use it, the Pouch proves that the smallest details often make the biggest difference.


Example:



Phone, keys, wallet, mints, sunglasses, chapstick etc.


Computer charger, cables, mouse


Tool kit


Toiletries

before.headline: Urban Cycling in Fall – What to Pack and Wear
before.articleBody:
There’s something special about riding through the city in the fall. The air feels crisp, the trees start to turn, and the bustle of urban life takes on a cozier rhythm. But while autumn brings some of the best days to be on a bike, it also requires a little extra thought when it comes to what you wear and what you carry. The mornings can be chilly, afternoons warmer, and evenings windy or damp. The right setup can make your rides smooth, comfortable, and enjoyable all season long.
What to Wear
Layer Smartly
Fall weather can change fast, so layering is your best friend. Start with a breathable base layer that wicks sweat. Add a lightweight long sleeve or sweatshirt, and finish with a windproof or water-resistant jacket. You can shed layers as the day warms up and pack them away easily.
I’m a huge fan of not having to change when I get to the office; I just want to lock up my bike and walk to my desk. In the summer, I can wear a dress or skirt with bike shorts underneath, but when the colder months come it gets a little harder to do that. I’ve found with the right layering and styling you can still wear a cute outfit without having to change.
My office can be a bit chilly all year round so I always have an extra sweater at the office but when the weather gets colder outside I typically wear a combination of pants and short sleeves paired with a knit sweater, and then I layer that with a cotton chore coat or tench coat; this system keeps me warm but doesn’t scream “I rode my bike to work,” and it allows me to take off layers when it gets too warm. Sometimes when I want to wear a skirt I will style my outfit, wear leggings on the ride, and put my skirt in my bag. Then when I get to the office, I can just pull the skirt over the leggings, and I’m ready to go. If the forecast calls for rain I just switch out the more fashionable coat for my rain coat. When it starts getting below 40 in the mornings I start laying my base layers under my pants, or sometimes I’ll wear my rain pants; I can pop those over almost any office outfit (even a dress). 
Protect Your Extremities
A thin pair of gloves makes a huge difference on those cool morning rides. A lightweight cap under your helmet keeps your head warm without overheating. As temperatures drop later in the season, consider wool socks to keep your feet cozy.
I personally love Bar Mitts. They might make your bike look a little bulky, but I prefer them over gloves because you have better control over your breaks. I’ve been in many situations where I had to quickly put on my breaks and slipped a little due to my gloves.

Urban cycling in the fall is about balance—staying warm without overheating, being prepared without overpacking, and embracing the season without letting the weather catch you off guard. With a thoughtful setup, you’ll find that autumn is one of the best times to enjoy the city by bike.

before.headline: The Art of Packing Light – Commuter Edition
before.articleBody:
A guide to efficient packing, smart design, and thoughtful organization for everyday riders.
Whether you’re biking to work, hopping on public transit, or weaving through the city on foot, packing light is one of the greatest gifts you can give your commute. The less you carry, the more freedom you feel. And with the right system, packing light doesn’t mean sacrificing what you need—it means carrying exactly what matters, in a way that feels effortless.
For many riders looking to upgrade their everyday setup—or find the best bike bags investment for the holiday season—packing light starts with choosing gear that supports efficiency instead of adding bulk.
Pack With Purpose: A Guide to Efficient Commuter Packing
Efficient packing starts with knowing your essentials. For most commuters, the daily carry list includes a laptop or tablet, keys, phone, wallet, maybe a lunch or water bottle, and a few personal items. The goal isn’t to cut that list down to nothing; the goal is to eliminate the extras that add weight and clutter.
Here’s how to streamline your setup:


Create a daily carry checklist. Knowing what truly needs to leave the house with you prevents “just in case” items from sneaking in.


Choose versatile essentials. A slim tech organizer for cables and chargers, or a compact reusable tote for groceries or lunch, ensures every item pulls double duty—reducing what you need to carry.


Build a consistent system. Designate pockets or compartments for each item so nothing ends up floating loose or forgotten.


The more predictable your packing routine becomes, the smoother your commute feels—especially when paired with quality cycling gear that’s designed to work with your lifestyle, not against it.
How Good Design Reduces What You Need to Carry
A well-designed commuter bag doesn’t just hold your belongings—it actively helps you carry less.
Thoughtful bag design can eliminate redundant pouches, protective sleeves, and extra organizers by integrating those features directly into the core structure of the bag. Built-in padding for your laptop means ditching a bulky case. Structured pockets for everyday essentials mean no need for extra accessory bags. Quick-access exterior pockets keep your most-used items right at your fingertips.
A good commuter bag should:


Protect what you carry so you can leave extra cases at home


Offer intuitive organization that keeps things where you expect


Shift comfortably between commuting modes—bike, walk, train


Feel lightweight even when loaded through balanced, ergonomic design


Choosing durable bike accessories with these built-in advantages naturally shortens your packing list and simplifies your daily routine. This is why investing in well-crafted bags—like those from small makers focused on function-first design—pays off year after year.
Thoughtful Organization: The Key to Packing Light
Packing light isn’t just about carrying less—it’s about carrying smarter. Thoughtful organization ensures every item has a place, reducing clutter and eliminating the need for excess gear.
Consider these organizational habits:


Keep small items together. Use a designated pocket for keys, chapstick, pens, and earbuds instead of separate pouches.


Prioritize quick access. Put your most-used items closest to the exterior so you’re not unpacking your entire bag to find one thing.


Use vertical space. Stack items upright to maximize room and maintain balance on your bike or shoulder.


Reset daily. A quick nightly tidy keeps your system running smoothly.


Combining smart habits with a thoughtfully crafted commuter bag transforms the way you travel—making your daily carry lighter, more intentional, and far more enjoyable.
Why Garner and Tow Makes the “Best Bike Bags Investment” List This Holiday Season

Each design is built with the needs of real riders in mind—blending durability, intuitive organization, and clean, versatile styling that works both on and off the bike.

Transition seamlessly off the bike

A versatile, lightweight bag


Easy access pockets

before.headline: The 5 Items I Never Ride Without
before.articleBody:
If I’m being honest, there are a few things that are obviously non-negotiable when you leave the house on a bike: phone, keys, and wallet. If you don’t have those, the ride’s kind of over before it starts.
When I designed my Garner & Tow bags, I made sure those everyday essentials were easy to access, secure, and not floating around loosely — because fumbling at a stoplight or digging through a bag on the sidewalk is not the vibe.
Once those basics are covered, these are the five things I personally never ride without.
 

 
1. A Lock (Peace of mind > everything)
Even if I’m “just popping in for a minute,” I’m not leaving my bike unlocked.
How the bag handles it: The bag is built to comfortably carry heavier items like a U-lock or chain without throwing off balance. The weight sits close to the bike when riding and stays comfortable on your body once you’re off.


 
2. Sunglasses or Clear Glasses
Light changes fast — especially during early morning or evening rides. I almost always carry an extra pair because my eyes are sensitive to wind, and that extra protection makes a huge difference in how comfortable the ride feels. Not squinting or dealing with watery eyes means I can actually stay focused on the road instead of just pushing through it.
How the bag handles it:
The structured shape protects fragile items without needing a bulky hard case, and the front slip pockets make it easy to quickly stash or grab my glasses on the go. I can slide them in at a stoplight or pull them out mid-ride without unpacking the whole bag — and trust they’ll stay protected.


 
3. Headphones (for before + after the ride)
I don’t ride with traditional headphones in — I always want my road-side ear open for safety. Bone-conduction headphones are a game changer because they let me hear directions or music while still staying aware of traffic, bells, and everything happening around me. Once I lock up, they’re still easy to grab and go.
How the bag handles it: A secure internal pocket keeps small tech from getting lost or crushed, so they’re always easy to grab when I need them.
 

 
4. Option A: Refillable Water Bottle
(Practical, everyday rider energy) Hydration is one of those things you don’t think about until you really need it — especially on longer rides or warm days.

How the bag handles it: The side pockets are designed to comfortably fit both large and small water bottles, keeping them upright and easy to reach without shifting around while you ride.


 
5. One “Just in Case” Item
This changes day to day — a snack, lip balm, sunscreen, hand wipes, or whatever I didn’t think I’d need until I absolutely did.
How the bag handles it: There’s room for the little extras without everything turning into a mess. The layout keeps items organized but adaptable.
 

 
Why I Designed the Bag This Way
I didn’t set out to make a hyper-technical bike bag. I wanted something that worked for real rides — commuting, errands, meeting friends, living life — without forcing me to change how I move once I’m off the bike.
This bag attaches when you’re riding, wears comfortably when you’re walking, and carries exactly what you need — nothing more, nothing less.
If you ride to get places (not just miles), this bag was made for you.

before.headline: Why We Made The Everyday Line
before.articleBody:
When we started Garner and Tow, the goal was simple: build bags that could keep up with how people actually move through the world. Not just on a bike—but beyond it. Bags that didn’t ask you to choose between function and form, or between riding and living.
Over time, we noticed something.
A lot of people weren’t heading out on multi-day rides or weekend trips—they were commuting. Riding to work. Meeting friends after. Stopping at the grocery store on the way home. Their rides were shorter, but more frequent. More integrated into daily life.
And while our original designs could absolutely handle that, we realized something important: daily riders deserve gear that’s purpose-built for them.
That’s where The Everyday Line comes in.
What Stayed the Same
We didn’t start from scratch. We refined it.
At the core, The Everyday Line is still everything Garner and Tow stands for.
Materials. We continue to use durable waxed canvas because it performs in real conditions. It sheds water, wears in—not out—and tells a story over time. If you’re looking for a waxed canvas commuter bag, this is exactly what that should feel like: reliable, weather-ready, and built to last.
Chicago production. Every bag is still made here in Chicago. That proximity matters. It allows us to stay hands-on with production, maintain consistency, and support the kind of manufacturing ecosystem we believe in. A Chicago bike bag should reflect the city it comes from—resilient, hardworking, and built for all seasons.
Construction standards. We didn’t cut corners to make something “simpler.” The Everyday Line holds the same construction principles as our more adventure-oriented gear: reinforced stress points, thoughtful stitching, and hardware that can take repeated use. These bags are meant to be used every day—and to hold up when you do.
What Changed
Designing an everyday bike bag isn’t about making something smaller. It’s about making something smarter.
Size and scale. The Everyday Line is more compact by design. You don’t need 20+ liters for a daily commute—but you do need the right amount of space, organized well. These bags are sized to carry your essentials without feeling bulky when you’re off the bike.
Mounting system. We focused on making the on-and-off transition seamless. Whether you’re locking up outside a café or heading into the office, the mounting system is intuitive and secure—no fiddling, no second-guessing.
Feature set for daily utility. This is where the biggest shift happened. We designed with daily friction points in mind:


Dedicated storage for a laptop, making it a true bike pannier laptop solution


Easy-access pockets for the things you reach for constantly


Carry options that feel natural once you’re off the bike


Because the reality is, most of your day isn’t spent riding. Your bag needs to work just as well when you’re walking into a meeting as it does when you’re pedaling there.
An Expansion, Not a Compromise
The Everyday Line isn’t a step away from what we’ve been doing—it’s a step deeper into it.
We’re still building adaptable bags. Still focused on the intersection of movement and daily life. The difference is that now, we’re speaking more directly to the rider who’s out there every single day.
This line exists because that kind of consistency deserves better design.
Not more features. Not more bulk. Just the right ones.
And as always, built to move with you.

before.headline: Handlebar Bag vs. Rear Rack Bag: Which Setup Is Right for You?
before.articleBody:
If you commute, run errands, or ride daily, your bike bag setup shapes how your ride feels. Weight distribution, accessibility, and how the bag transitions off the bike all play a role in choosing the right system.
Two of the most popular options are handlebar bags and rear rack bags (panniers). Both solve the same problem—carrying your daily essentials—but they do it in very different ways.
This guide breaks down the pros, tradeoffs, and best use cases so you can choose the right setup for your riding style.
 

 
Why Bike Bag Placement Matters
Where your bag sits on the bike changes:


How your bike handles


How quickly you can access your gear


How comfortable the bag is off the bike


How much weight you can carry


There isn’t a universal “best” option—only the best option for how you ride.
 

 
Handlebar Bag: Quick Access + Everyday Convenience
A handlebar bag mounts to the front of your bike and keeps your essentials within arm’s reach while riding.
Think of it as the bike equivalent of a daily carry bag.
Best for:


Short to medium commutes


Coffee runs and errands


Minimal everyday carry


Riders without a rear rack


Pros of a Handlebar Bag
1. Fast Access While Riding
Phone, wallet, snacks, keys—everything is visible and reachable without stopping. This is the biggest reason many daily riders prefer a handlebar setup.
2. Simpler Bike Setup
No rack required. Mounting is quick and minimal, making it ideal for road bikes, gravel bikes, or minimalist commuters.
3. Easy Transition Off the Bike
Handlebar bags typically convert easily into crossbody or shoulder bags, making them perfect for stop-and-go city riding.
4. Great for Light Loads
Perfect capacity for daily essentials without encouraging overpacking.
Tradeoffs of Handlebar Bags


Limited capacity compared to rear rack bags


Heavy loads can affect steering feel


Not ideal for laptops + large gear loads


 

 
Rear Rack Bag (Pannier): Stability + Carrying Capacity
A rear rack bag commuter setup moves the weight behind the rider, creating a more stable ride—especially when carrying heavier items.
If your bike bag needs to function like a mobile office or grocery hauler, this is where rear rack bags shine.
Best for:


Longer commutes


Carrying laptops or work gear


Grocery runs and errands


Heavier daily loads


Pros of Rear Rack Bags
1. Better Weight Distribution
Placing weight over the rear wheel keeps steering light and predictable. This matters most when carrying heavier loads.
2. More Storage Capacity
Rear rack bags typically hold significantly more than handlebar bags—ideal for laptops, lunch, clothing layers, or groceries.
3. Comfortable for Longer Rides
Because the weight sits low and centered, the bike feels balanced even when fully loaded.
4. Ideal for Daily Commuters
This setup is popular among year-round riders who carry work gear regularly.
Tradeoffs of Rear Rack Bags


Requires installing a rack


Gear is less accessible while riding


Can feel oversized for quick trips


 

 
Which Setup Is Right for Your Commute?
Choose a handlebar bag if:
You carry essentials, make frequent stops, and want the fastest on/off bike transition.
This setup excels for riders who treat their bike like a daily mobility tool.
Choose a rear rack bag if:
Your bike carries your workday. Laptop, lunch, layers, groceries—this setup handles heavier loads comfortably.
 

 
The Flexible Middle Ground
Many riders eventually use both positions depending on the ride.
A versatile system lets you:


Mount up front for quick errands


Move to the rear rack for heavier commutes


Wear the same bag off the bike


This flexibility is what makes adaptable bike bags especially useful for everyday riders.
 

 
Final Thoughts: Match the Bag to the Ride
The best bike bag mounting option is the one that matches your daily routine.


Quick rides → Handlebar bag


Heavy commuting → Rear rack bag


Mixed riding → Versatile mounting options


Choosing the right setup isn’t about carrying more—it’s about carrying smarter.

before.headline: What to Pack in Your Bike Commuter Bag (And How to Organize It)
before.articleBody:
Whether you're riding across town to work, running errands after a coffee stop, or heading out for a weekend adventure, having a well-organized bike commuter bag can make every ride smoother. The right gear helps you stay prepared without overpacking, and a thoughtful organization system means you can find what you need when you need it.
Here's our guide to building the perfect bike commuter bag packing list and organizing it for different types of rides.
The Essentials: What to Carry on Your Bike Commute
No matter where you're headed, a few items belong in every commuter setup:


Wallet or card holder


Keys


Phone


Water bottle


Bike lock


Mini bike tool or multi-tool


Spare tube or flat repair kit


Compact hand pump or CO₂ inflator


Sunglasses


Lightweight layer or rain jacket


Chapstick


Snacks


These essentials cover most daily rides and help you handle common situations without carrying unnecessary weight.
Scenario 1: The Work Day Commute
For riders heading to the office, organization is key. You need easy access to daily essentials while keeping work items protected and separate.
Packed in the Crescent
The Crescent’s larger capacity makes it ideal for carrying work gear while keeping everything secure on the bike.
What to pack:


Laptop or tablet


Notebook


Chargers and cables


Water bottle


Lunch


Light jacket


Wallet, keys, and phone


Flat repair kit


Organization Tips
Use smaller pouches to group similar items together:


Electronics in one pouch


Bike repair essentials in another


Personal items in a dedicated pocket


This prevents your bag from becoming a catch-all and makes it easy to grab what you need once you arrive at work.
Scenario 2: The Everyday Errand Run
Sometimes you don't need to carry your entire day with you. For quick trips around town, a lighter setup is often the most convenient.
Packed in the Satchel
The Satchel is perfect for carrying everyday essentials while staying compact and comfortable off the bike.
What to pack:


Wallet


Phone


Keys


Sunglasses


Reusable shopping bag


Water bottle


Small snack


Compact lock


The streamlined size encourages you to bring only what you need while still leaving room for a few unexpected purchases.
Organization Tips
Place frequently used items—phone, wallet, and keys—in the front pocket. Reserve the main compartment for bulkier items like a reusable shopping bag or light layer.
Scenario 3: The Weekend Ride
Weekend rides often blend transportation and adventure. You may stop for coffee, visit a market, meet friends, or explore a new neighborhood.
Crescent + Satchel Setup
Combining both bags gives you flexibility throughout the day.
What to pack in the Satchel:


Extra layer


Water bottle


Snacks


Camera


Flat repair kit


Lightweight rain shell


What to pack in the Crescent:


Phone


Wallet


Keys


Small personal items


This setup keeps valuables close while allowing larger items to stay mounted on the bike.
Commuter Bag Organization Tips
1. Create Zones
Think of your bag as having dedicated areas:


Daily essentials


Work gear


Bike tools


Food and hydration


When every item has a home, you spend less time digging through your bag.
2. Use Pouches
Small organizers help prevent loose items from collecting at the bottom of your bag. They're especially useful for cables, tools, and personal care items.
3. Pack by Frequency
Items you use constantly should be easiest to reach. Things you rarely need can stay deeper in the bag.
4. Review Your Setup Regularly
If you've been carrying something for months without using it, consider removing it. A lighter bag makes every ride more enjoyable.
5. Prepare for Weather
A compact rain jacket or extra layer can make a huge difference. Weather can change quickly, especially during spring and fall commuting seasons.
Build a System That Works for You
The best bike commuter bag packing list is the one that supports your daily routine. Some riders prioritize carrying work gear, while others focus on flexibility for errands and social rides. The key is creating an organization system that makes your essentials easy to access and keeps unnecessary clutter out.
Whether you're packing the Crescent for a quick trip across town or loading up the Satchel for a full workday, thoughtful organization can make every ride more comfortable, efficient, and enjoyable.

after.name: How to Care for Waxed Canvas Bags

itemListElement.name: Remove dirt and debris
itemListElement.text: Gently brush dirt or debris off with a soft brush or cloth.

itemListElement.name: Clean stains
itemListElement.text: For stains, use a damp cloth with cold water. Avoid soap or detergents, as they can strip the wax coating.

itemListElement.name: Dry the bag
itemListElement.text: Allow the bag to air dry naturally and avoid heat sources like dryers or radiators.

itemListElement.name: Apply wax
itemListElement.text: Rub in wax evenly onto the fabric with a cloth.

itemListElement.name: Heat to absorb
itemListElement.text: Use a hairdryer or warm iron with parchment paper to help it absorb.

itemListElement.name: Store properly
itemListElement.text: Store the bag in a cool, dry place to prevent mildew, and avoid plastic bags.
